text: A matrix is the object that acts on the vectors from Chapter 1, and every quantum gate you'll ever apply is a matrix. Before you can understand what a gate does, you need to be fluent with three basic operations: addition, scalar multiplication, and — the one that matters most — matrix multiplication.

Matrix addition and scalar multiplication work entry by entry, exactly like vectors — add matching entries, or scale every entry by a number. Both operations are commutative. Matrix multiplication is where everything changes.

To multiply A times B, each entry of the result is the dot product of a row of A with a column of B. Working through A equals 2,3,1, negative 1 and B equals 1,0,4,2 gives AB equals 14,6, negative 3, negative 2. Multiply in the opposite order, BA, and you get 2,3,10,10 — a completely different matrix. A B does not equal B A. This is not a special case; it is the general rule.

A vector is just a matrix with one column, so the same row-times-column rule gives you a matrix acting on a state. This is the single most important fact for quantum computing: a circuit applying gate A then gate B is the matrix product B A, not A B, because matrices act right-to-left on the state they're given. Swap the order of two gates and you generally get a physically different final state — exactly why gate order in a circuit diagram is never arbitrary.

Next lesson makes the biggest conceptual leap in this chapter: seeing M v not as an arithmetic operation but as a rule that transforms v into a new vector — exactly what a quantum gate does to a qubit's state.
